resources.string: How the placenta exchanges gases and nutrients
Normal human placental anatomy and physiology in late pregnancy. The views and motion are schematic: not to scale and not a measure of flow or transfer.

The placenta lies against the uterine wall and connects to the fetus through the umbilical cord. On the fetal side, trees of chorionic villi branch into a space filled with maternal blood. The ring marks one of the fine tips, called terminal villi.

Maternal blood enters through uterine spiral arteries, flows around the villi in the intervillous space, and drains into uterine veins. Two umbilical arteries bring fetal blood to the villous capillaries; one umbilical vein returns it to the fetus. The two blood streams do not directly mix during normal exchange.
Look closely at the villous surface

The syncytiotrophoblast is a continuous outer layer with many nuclei that is in direct contact with maternal blood. Fetal blood remains within the capillary endothelium. Where the capillary hugs the surface, very little tissue separates the blood streams.

Oxygen moves overall from maternal blood to fetal blood; carbon dioxide moves overall in the opposite direction. They diffuse across the thin villous barrier down their respective partial-pressure gradients. The arrows show net transfer of gases, not the motion of blood cells.

Glucose is one example of a nutrient that moves overall toward fetal blood. GLUT1 proteins on both sides of the syncytiotrophoblast help glucose cross that layer by facilitated diffusion. Different nutrients can use different mechanisms.
